title: Dynamic Programming Check
description: Predict DP table values and identify overlapping subproblems vs. optimal substructure.

questions.prompt: What two properties must a problem have for Dynamic Programming to apply?

options.text: Sorted input and a single loop
Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
A graph structure and no cycles
Constant time lookups and recursion

questions.explanation: DP exploits overlapping subproblems (the same smaller problem recurs) combined with optimal substructure (the answer is built from smaller answers).

options.text: Because it uses a `for` loop internally
Because it recomputes the same subproblems (like `ways(3)`) many times across different recursive branches
Because JavaScript recursion is always slow
Because it uses an array instead of a table

questions.explanation: Without memoization or a table, each call branches into two more calls, and the same smaller subproblem gets solved repeatedly — this is the overlapping-subproblems cost.

questions.prompt: In `waysDP`, what does `table[i] = table[i - 1] + table[i - 2]` represent?

options.text: The number of ways to reach step `i`, built from the already-computed ways to reach `i-1` and `i-2`
A random initialization value
The total number of steps taken so far
An error-checking formula

questions.explanation: The last step taken to reach `i` was either a single step from `i-1` or a double step from `i-2` — summing those two already-solved subproblems gives `ways(i)`.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of `waysDP(n)` compared to `waysNaive(n)`?

options.text: `waysDP` is `O(n)`; `waysNaive` is `O(2^n)`
Both are `O(n)`
`waysDP` is `O(n^2)`; `waysNaive` is `O(n)`
Both are `O(2^n)`

questions.explanation: `waysDP` fills each subproblem once in a single pass (`O(n)`); `waysNaive` re-solves overlapping subproblems across an exponentially branching call tree (`O(2^n)`).

questions.prompt: Does DP change *what* is computed compared to the naive recursive formula, or *how* it is computed?

options.text: It changes what is computed — DP uses a different recurrence
It changes how it is computed — the same recurrence is filled bottom-up and reused instead of recomputed
It changes neither; DP is purely a naming convention
It replaces recursion with sorting

questions.explanation: The recurrence `ways(i) = ways(i-1) + ways(i-2)` is identical in both versions; DP only changes the computation strategy from repeated recursive calls to a single bottom-up table fill.
